{{Short description|Generalization of polynomials}}
{{For multi|quasi-polynomial bounds in the analysis of algorithms|Quasi-polynomial growth|functions that take the form of polynomials in a variable and an exponential function|Exponential polynomial}}
{{one source |date=May 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''quasi-polynomial''' (sometimes called '''pseudo-polynomial''') is a generalization of [[polynomial]]s. While the coefficients of a polynomial come from a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]], the coefficients of quasi-polynomials are instead [[periodic function]]s with integral period. Quasi-polynomials appear throughout much of [[combinatorics]] as the enumerators for various objects.

==Definition==
A '''quasi-polynomial''' is a function <math>q</math> defined on <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> of the form <math>q(n) = c_d(n) n^d + c_{d-1}(n) n^{d-1} + \cdots + c_0(n)</math>, where each <math>c_i(n)</math> is a [[periodic function]] with integral period. If <math>c_d(n)</math> is not identically zero, then the '''degree''' of <math>q</math> is <math>d</math>, and any common period of <math>c_0(n), c_1(n), \dots, c_d(n)</math> is a '''period''' of <math>q</math>.
The minimal such period (sometimes simply called <i>the</i> period or the '''quasi-period''' of <math>q</math>) is the [[least common multiple]] of the periods of <math>c_0(n), c_1(n), \dots, c_d(n)</math>.

Equivalently, a function <math>q</math> defined on <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is a quasi-polynomial if there exist a positive integer <math>s</math> and polynomials <math>p_0, \dots, p_{s-1}</math> such that <math>q(n) = p_i(n)</math> when <math>i \equiv n \bmod s</math>. The minimal such <math>s</math> coincides with the minimal period of <math>q</math>.
The polynomials <math>p_i</math> are called the '''constituents''' of <math>q</math>.

==Generating functions==

A function <math>q</math> defined on <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is a quasi-polynomial of degree <math>\le d</math> and period dividing <math>r</math> if and only its [[generating function]]

:: <math>Q(x) := \sum_{ n \ge 0 } q(n) x^n </math>

evaluates to a rational function of the form <math>Q(x) = \frac{ h(x) }{ (1-x^r)^{ d+1 } }</math> where <math>h(x)</math> is a polynomial of degree <math> < r(d+1)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stanley |first=Richard P. |author-link=Richard P. Stanley |date=1997 |chapter=Section 4.4: Quasipolynomials |title=Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1 |url=http://www-math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-56069-1}}</ref><ref name=becksanyal>{{citation
 | last1 = Beck | first1 = Matthias
 | last2 = Sanyal | first2 = Raman
 | chapter=Section 4.5: Quasipolynomials
 | isbn = 978-1-4704-2200-4
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = [[Graduate Studies in Mathematics]]
 | title = Combinatorial Reciprocity Theorems: An Invitation to Enumerative Geometric Combinatorics
 | year = 2018}}</ref>
Thus quasi-polynomials are characterized through generating functions that are rational and whose poles are rational roots of unity.

==Examples==
* Given a <math>d</math>-dimensional [[convex polytope]] <math>P</math> with [[rational number|rational]] vertices <math>v_1,\dots,v_n</math>, define <math>tP</math> to be the [[convex hull]] of <math>tv_1,\dots,tv_n</math>. The function <math>L(P,t) = \#(tP \cap \mathbb{Z}^d)</math> is a quasi-polynomial in <math>t</math> (viewed as a positive integer variable) of degree <math>d</math>; the minimal positive integer <math>r</math> such that <math>r P</math> has integer vertices is a period of <math>L(P,t)</math>. This is known as the [[Ehrhart quasi-polynomial]], named after [[Eugène Ehrhart]].
* Given two quasi-polynomials <math>F</math> and <math>G</math>, the [[convolution]] of <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> is
:: <math>(F*G)(k) = \sum_{m=0}^k F(m)G(k-m)</math>
:which is a quasi-polynomial with degree <math>\le \deg F + \deg G + 1.</math>
